common_name: Golden Delicious Pineapple Sage (Golden Pineapple Sage)

planting.note: Set out transplants or rooted cuttings after all danger of frost, in rich, well-drained soil; this cultivar is grown as much for its bright chartreuse-gold foliage as for its late-fall scarlet flowers.

directions: Plant in a bed with morning sun and afternoon shade in the Gulf Coast heat, since strong all-day sun can bleach the golden foliage. Pinch stems through summer to keep growth bushy and to delay the tubular red flower spikes, which appear in October and November and are a major late-season hummingbird draw. Foliage and flowers carry a strong pineapple fragrance and are edible, used in teas and as a garnish. In zone 8 protect the crown with mulch over winter; it usually returns from the roots even if top growth is killed by frost.

planting.note: Set out nursery starts after frost danger has passed in well-drained, amended beds or large containers; this Australian-bred hybrid blooms nearly nonstop through the hot, humid Gulf Coast season.

directions: This vigorous chance seedling produces magenta-pink flowers with wine-colored calyces on sprawling, arching stems from spring through frost. Give it full sun and good drainage; it tolerates heat and humidity better than many salvias and is a strong hummingbird and butterfly plant for Gulf Coast borders. Cut back hard in late winter to renew growth, and take softwood cuttings in fall as insurance since plants can be short-lived in wet winter soils. In colder zone 8 pockets treat as a root-hardy perennial and mulch the crown heavily.

common_name: Black and Bloom Salvia (Bigger, Bolder Hummingbird Sage)

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery starts after last frost in humus-rich, evenly moist soil; this selection outperforms the older 'Black and Blue' with larger flowers and near-black stems and calyces.

directions: Site in full sun to light afternoon shade with consistently moist, fertile soil for the strongest bloom and darkest calyx color; this cultivar was bred for improved vigor and larger deep-cobalt flowers compared with the classic 'Black and Blue'. It spreads by rhizomes to form a dense clump and is one of the top hummingbird plants for late summer into fall in Gulf Coast gardens. In zone 8 the top growth is killed by hard freezes but the roots reliably resprout in spring under a thick mulch layer; further south it stays evergreen.

common_name: Assam Orange Ginger Lily (Orange Bottlebrush Ginger)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring once soil has warmed, in rich, moisture-retentive soil; unlike the more common butterfly gingers, this species produces dense orange bottlebrush-shaped flower spikes rather than large fragrant blooms.

directions: Grow in dappled shade to morning sun with consistently moist, organically rich soil; this selection of Hedychium densiflorum is valued for its compact, densely packed orange-red flower spikes in mid to late summer, held above lush cane-like foliage. It is one of the more cold-tolerant ginger lily species, and clumps in zone 8 typically survive winter with a heavy mulch layer even when top growth is frozen back. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in early spring to maintain vigorous flowering.

common_name: Tara Ginger Lily (Hardy Scarlet Ginger Lily)

planting.note: Set out divisions in spring after soil has warmed in fertile, well-watered beds; Tara is among the most cold-hardy ginger lily selections and one of the more reliable for the cooler edge of zone 8.

directions: Plant in a spot with morning sun and afternoon shade and keep the soil consistently moist through summer for tall stands of orange-red flower spikes from late summer into fall. Tara was selected for its exceptional winter hardiness among Hedychium coccineum forms, making it a good choice for gardeners near the zone 8a/8b line. Mulch heavily after the first freeze knocks back the foliage, and divide dense clumps every few years to renew bloom and share plants.

common_name: Red King Humbert Canna (Classic Bronze-Leaf Heirloom Canna)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes after danger of frost has passed, 3-4 inches deep in rich, heavily amended soil; this early-1900s heirloom pairs bold bronze-maroon foliage with large orange-red flowers.

directions: Give this heirloom canna full sun and steady moisture, including standing water at pond margins where it thrives. Introduced in the early 1900s, it remains one of the most widely grown bronze-leaved cannas for its combination of dark maroon-red foliage and vivid orange-scarlet blooms that appear from summer through fall. Deadhead spent flower stalks to prolong bloom, and in zone 8 either mulch heavily to overwinter rhizomes in place or lift and store them after the first killing frost. Divide congested clumps every two to three years to keep flowering strong.

common_name: Ann Chowning Louisiana Iris (Historic White Louisiana Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly in early fall in humus-rich, constantly moist soil so roots establish before the spring bloom flush; this classic white-flowered selection is part of the historic Chowning breeding line of Louisiana irises.

directions: Set rhizomes just below the soil surface in a bog bed, rain garden, or pond margin with rich organic soil, since Louisiana irises perform best with abundant moisture during spring growth. Ann Chowning produces clean white blooms with a bright yellow signal in mid-spring and is prized for naturalizing in the wet, humid conditions typical of Gulf Coast gardens. Feed lightly in late winter as growth resumes, and divide crowded clumps every three to four years after bloom to maintain vigor. Reduce watering somewhat in the dormant summer period if grown outside standing water.

common_name: Common Yellow Plumeria (Traditional Hawaiian Yellow Frangipani)

planting.note: Root hardwood cuttings in well-drained, gritty potting mix and move outdoors only after nights stay reliably above 50°F; this old, widely naturalized cultivar is the classic fragrant lei-flower yellow-and-white plumeria.

directions: Grow in full sun in fast-draining soil or a large container, since waterlogged roots are the main cause of failure; along the Gulf Coast this cultivar is best grown in a pot that can be moved to a garage or greenhouse for winter dormancy. Common Yellow produces intensely fragrant white flowers with golden-yellow centers from late spring through fall and is among the most widely propagated and lei-grade plumerias in Hawaii and the tropics. Withhold water almost entirely once the plant drops its leaves and goes dormant in winter storage, and resume watering only after new growth appears in spring.
